This paper proposes a new comprehensive benchmark for evaluating multi-modal image generation, consisting of a dataset and evaluation framework, including a new quality metric. The benchmark unifies text-to-image and image-conditioned evaluation, and is supported by a large-scale study of human preferences. Reviewers emphasize that this addresses an important gap in today's image generation benchmarks. Some concerns were raised about the computional cost of the newly proposed metric, but these were sufficiently addressed by the authors through enabling the use of a smaller size model. Other concerns around dataset size/quality and model coverage were similarly addressed through clarifications and additional experiments. The consensus among the reviewers is that this represents a solid contribution that will be very useful to the community. I agree and enthusiastically propose accepting the paper.

===== FINAL UPDATE FROM DB Track PCs ====

The final decision for this paper has been taken by the program chairs after consultation with the SACs. All Senior Area Chairs have ranked papers according to the feedback from the AC during the review process. We decided to leave the original meta-review to reflect the opinion of the AC in light of the initial discussions with reviewers and SAC.

Dear Reviewer 4biR,

Thank you so much for your thoughtful follow-up and for acknowledging that most of your concerns have been addressed. We appreciate your recognition of the practical considerations in our evaluation methodology and the value of our multi-dimensional evaluation framework. **Since you feel your main concerns have been resolved, we would be grateful if you could reflect this in your final score**, as it would help recognize the contributions and utility of our work for the community.

Thank you again for your time and consideration!

Best,

Authors

**Dear Reviewer 4biR,**

Thank you so much for your thoughtful comments. We are pleased to address your remaining concerns.

To provide further clarity on the computational efficiency of AMS, we report that the FLOPS of Qwen-VL2.5-72B is **103,895.795 GFLOPs**.

In addition, we would like to highlight that **Qwen-VL2.5-72B is available as an API deployed on Alibaba Cloud**, enabling users to access its capabilities without local deployment or significant hardware investment.

We also experimented with a smaller, more accessible 7B model that can be deployed on a single GPU for AMS calculation. While this reduces computational requirements, our results indicate that the correlation with human judgments is slightly lower than that of the 72B model (please also see the results in the response to Reviewer NDn2 Q3). However, it still surpasses the performance of DSG. The Qwen2VL-7B results are summarized below:

- **Spearman rank correlation**: 0.70 (_p_ = 0.011)
- **Kendall tau**: 0.54 (_p_ = 0.012)

As for the AMS metric, we extract compositional aspects (objects, attributes, relations, numbers) from the text prompts and generate the QA pairs with GPT-4o, followed by human revision. In contrast, for DSG, prompts are directly parsed into scene graphs by GPT-3 without human validation or revision. This human-in-the-loop approach ensures higher evaluation quality and better alignment with human judgment, as evidenced by our correlation results. 

We believe this computational investment is justified by AMS's unique capability for interpretable, aspect-level evaluation that enables fine-grained model diagnosis, which is not available in faster traditional metrics. We sincerely hope this addresses your concerns and clarifies the trade-offs between efficiency and evaluation alignment.

We thank the reviewer for the helpful comments and provide our responses below:
> More details on user study: the actual annotation guidelines and inter-annotator agreement statistics are not fully described.

Please see Sec. A.8, and Fig. 12-16 of the Appendix. The figures show user interfaces and annotation instructions.

For the user study on the prompt-following evaluation, the inter-annotator agreement rate is 77.47%. We will add the complete statistics to the revised paper.

> More details on data filtering: the process of prompt/manual verification for toxic/ambiguous content, and quality control criteria for image selection, remain somewhat abstract.

1. Image selection: We asked professional users to collect the images from a website of free stock images. They manually filtered out images with toxic contents (e.g., violence and sexual contents). To ensure the quality, they mainly followed the criteria below:
   - High resolution;
   - Diversity: in each image group, the subject should have notable view/pose changes;
   - Complexity: the main object in the image should have complex textures.

2. Prompt verification: We manually went through all generated text prompts and filtering out the prompts with toxic contents.

> Insufficient model comparison: (1) RealCustom; (2) Less-to-more generalization.

We show additional quantitative comparisons in the table below:

| Model      | CLIP-T  | CLIP-I  | Dinov2  | CUTE    | PAL4VST | BLIPVQA | AMS    | Aesthetic | HPSv2  | PickScore |
|------------|---------|---------|---------|---------|---------|---------|--------|-----------|--------|------------|
| UNO        | 31.439  | 75.194  | 23.079  | 65.808  | 3.060   | 0.539   | 67.94  | 6.1563    | 0.2712 | 0.0865     |
| RealCustom | 31.596  | 73.236  | 22.678  | 67.132  | 2.517   | 0.533   | 63.77  | 6.1327    | 0.2910 | 0.0943     |
| OmniGen    | 33.178  | 72.327  | 21.380  | 56.666  | 2.908   | 0.588   | 73.52  | 6.0859    | 0.2963 | 0.1521     |

As suggested by reviewer 4biR, we also compared to OmniGen.

> How the three levels are divided, since both mid level and high level includes human-aligned evaluation.

1. Low-level metrics mainly focus on the local appearances of the generated images, including identity details (e.g., textures, local structures) and local artifacts.
2. Mid-level metrics correspond to four aspects of semantics: object, relation, attribute, and counting. The human-aligned metric at this level is more fine-grained and provide detailed interpretability.
3. High-level metrics evaluate overall aesthetics and human preference. Different with the mid-level metrics, the human-aligned metric at this level only suggests a general and abstract preference on the quality. It is not interpretable.

> In table 1, the CLIP-T metrics of existing methods are very close.

CLIP-T is not sensitive to fine-grained semantics of the text. It may often assign highly-similar scores for images that match a high-level topic but diferentiate in key details. Furthermore, it is not able to capture relation, attribute, and counting. These all contribute to the observation that the performance between different models is close. However, we still include it, as it is a widely-used score for measuring both text-to-image and customized generation tasks.

We thank the reviewer for the helpful comments and provide our responses below:
> The benchmark does not have a metric measuring the diversity.

Thank you for highlighting the importance of using a metric to evaluate the diversity of generated images. In the customization task, we generate three images for each pair of reference image and text prompt. We then calculate the pairwise LPIPS scores among the three outputs and averaged them to obtain the final diversity score (see the table below). A higher LPIPS score indicates greater diversity in the image customization results.

|       | BLIP Diffusion | DreamBooth | Emu2 | Ip-Adapter-XL | MS Diffusion | UNO | RealCustom | OmniGen|
|------------|---------|---------|---------|---------|---------|---------|--------|-----------|
| LPIPS      |  0.5794 | 0.4322  | 0.3443  |  0.4532 |  0.5115 | 0.4696  | 0.5193 |   0.4679  |

> A deeper analysis of the leaderboard would be expected.

Thank you for pointing this out. We summarize some common design choices shared by the top-ranked text to image generation models and image customization models.

1. Model capacity: Winning diffusion models, such as HiDream-I1 17B, FLUX.1-dev 12B and SD3.5-large 10B, scale parameters aggressively. It indicates that larger model capacity correlates with higher AMS and human preference scores.

2. Visual token processing: Models with better visual understanding often incorporate more sophisticated visual encoders or resampling mechanisms, such as MS-Diffusion, which enhances their ability to preserve identity and capture nuanced visual details. This is especially evident in customization tasks where models like DreamBooth, with multi-view fine-tuning, show strong identity preservation.

3. Architecture: Diffusion models consistently beat autoregressive models on artifact rate(PAL4VST) and aesthetics(Aesthetic). Current results show that autoregressive models still struggle with identity coherence. This might be due to challenges in balancing language modeling objectives with pixel-level visual generation, especially when dealing with variable-length decoding and fixed-size image output.

4. Training: A good training method is typically conducted with images of varying resolutions, beginning with low-resolution images and gradually moving to higher resolutions. This progressive approach helps improve the model's overall performance.[1]

We will include that information in the revision.

[1]:HiDream-I1: A High-Efficient Image Generative Foundation Model with Sparse Diffusion Transformer

> The calculation of AMS entails inference with Qwen-VL2.5-72B multiple times. This is super computationally expensive.

Thank you for highlighting the computational cost of AMS. To address this concern, we note that **Qwen-VL2.5-72B is available as an API deployed on Alibaba Cloud**, allowing users to leverage its capabilities without requiring local deployment or significant hardware resources.

We also experimented with using a smaller model 7B model for AMS calculation. While this reduces computational requirements, our results show that the correlation with human judgments is lower than with the 72B model (please also check the results in the response for Reviewer 4biR Q2). The Qwen2VL-7B performance is listed below:

- **Spearman rank correlation**: 0.70 (*p* = 0.011)
- **Kendall tau**: 0.54 (*p* = 0.012)

Therefore, there is a clear trade-off between computational efficiency and alignment with human judgment. We will include these findings and detailed correlation results in the revised version for greater transparency.

> It would make the paper more self-contained if the authors could provide a brief introduction of the metrics such as CUTE, PAL4VST, Aesthetic, etc in the appendix.

We will add the specifications below to the revised appendix:

1. CUTE: Based on DINOv2, it is able to capture intrinsic object-centric features. We apply it to measure identity similarity.
2. PAL4VST: It calculates the ratio of the artifact region in the generated image.
3. Aesthetic: It is a linear estimator built on CLIP to predict the aesthetic quality of the generated images.

Thank you for your thoughtful feedback. We appreciate your recognition of our multi-level assessment framework and the unprecedented scale of our human evaluation, which together provide a thorough and robust benchmark for image generation models. We are encouraged by your positive remarks and address your specific concerns below:

> Limited metric novelty: The proposed AMS, reliant on the computationally intensive Qwen-VL2.5-72B, exhibits significantly slower inference speed and much higher memory demands.

While AMS is built upon strong existing models (Qwen-VL2.5-72B), its *novelty* lies in its **aspect-aware, compositional evaluation**—a capability not offered by traditional metrics. AMS enables fine-grained assessment of region-level and aspect-level attributes (e.g., color, gesture, material), which we find essential for advancing model evaluation beyond holistic or VQA-style metrics. This design addresses the community’s need for interpretable, aspect-level benchmarking, as discussed in our main text (Sec. 4.2).

> Limited metric novelty: AMS shows low correlation with human evaluations.

We respectfully clarify that **AMS achieves the highest correlation with human ratings among all the related VQA-based automatic metrics we tested**, according to both Spearman and Kendall correlation:

| Metric   | Spearman r ↑ | p-value ↓ | Kendall tau ↑ | p-value ↓ |
|----------|-------------|-----------|---------------|-----------|
| BLIPVQA  | 0.51        | 0.090     | 0.36          | 0.116     |
| VQ2      | 0.40        | 0.199     | 0.33          | 0.153     |

We add the table below, comparing our MMGen-Bench with previous multi-modal image generation benchmarks. As the table shows, our proposed benchmark greatly exceeds the scale of previous benchmarks. It has two advantages over the previous works:

1. It significantly expands the scale to 1750 images (**3 times** of CustomConcept101) and 4850 prompts (**3 times** of DreamBench++);
2. It expands the groups of paired images to 386 (**3 times** of CustomConcept101). In image customization, 3-5 *paired* images are often required for test-time optimization and inference. > Dataset quality issue: The images in image-conditioned generation exhibit excessive similarity.

We intentionally collect groups of similar images for the following reason:

One of the main tasks our work mainly aims at is image customization, which often requires 3-5 similar images of the same subject as test-time input. This task is first defined and introduced in DreamBooth. In the DreamBench dataset (proposed by DreamBooth), similar images are also collected in groups, which is necessary for the model to learn the identity during test-time optimization. We thank the reviewer for the helpful comments and provide our responses below:
> Why do we need a VQA-based metric to evaluate the image-generated task?

We developed AMS for the following reasons:

1. Better interpretability: It enables fine-grained assessment of region-level and aspect-level attributes (object, relation, attribute, and counting), which is necessary for advancing model evaluation beyond holistic or VQA-style metrics.
2. Such metric is commonly used in previous works, including T2I-CompBench++, GenAI-Bench, etc.

summary.value: This paper proposes a benchmark for evaluating text-and-image conditioned multimodal image generation models. The work introduces a dataset consisting of 4,850 annotated text prompts paired with 1,750 multi-view reference images spanning 380 subjects. For evaluation, the authors implement a three-level methodology assessing low-level artifacts, mid-level semantics, and high-level aesthetics. The benchmark additionally incorporates 32,000 human ratings comparing outputs from state-of-the-art models.

strengths_contributions.value:
1.The authors propose to evaluate image generation across three distinct levels (artifact, semantic, and aesthetic), providing a relatively thorough multi-level assessment framework.

2.The benchmark includes extensive human feedback results (32K human ratings comparing the state-of-the-art models), which are useful and exceed the scale of user studies in prior work.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1.Limited metric novelty: The evaluation metrics primarily integrate existing tools/models, offering insufficient novelty. The proposed Aspect Matching Score (AMS), reliant on the computationally intensive Qwen-VL2.5-72B, exhibits significantly slower inference speed and much higher memory demands than traditional algorithms (specific inference speed and memory requirements are needed to report). Furthermore, AMS shows low correlation with human evaluations. As in Table 3, it ranks Lumina-2, HunyuanDiT, Pixart-Sigma, Flux.1-dev, and SD 3.5-large above GPT-4o, contradicting human ratings where GPT-4o performs noticeably better.

2.Inadequate dataset comparision: The contribution of the new dataset is diminished by the lack of comparison with relevant existing datasets (e.g., Custom Diffusion [1], I2EBench [2]).

3.Incomplete model coverage: The evaluation omits relevant multi-modal generation models, such as FLUX-Redux [3] and Omnigen [4].

4.Dataset quality issue: The images in image-conditioned generation exhibit excessive similarity, impacting overall data quality.

5.Insufficient qualitative analysis: The paper lacks sufficient qualitative examples, especially for image-conditioned generation. More examples (especially in the main submission) are crucial for readers to assess the qualitative performance of the benchmarked multi-modal models.

Reference

[1] Kumari, Nupur, et al. "Multi-concept customization of text-to-image diffusion." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF conference on computer vision and pattern recognition. 2023.

[2] Ma, Yiwei, et al. "I2EBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Instruction-based Image Editing." The Thirty-eighth Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems. 2024.

[3] Black Forest Labs. "FLUX-Tools". https://bfl.ai/models/flux-tools. 2024.

[4] Xiao, Shitao, et al. "Omnigen: Unified image generation." Proceedings of the Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition Conference. 2025.

summary.value: The paper introduces MMGen-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating multi-modal image generation models, conditioned on both text and images. The benchmark pairs multi-view reference images with richly annotated text prompts, covering diverse categories such as compositionality, realism, and aesthetics. The authors propose a three-level evaluation framework to assess models at low-level, mid-level, and high-level. The benchmark is used to evaluate 17 models, providing insights into model strengths and limitations.

strengths_contributions.value:
I am not an expert in the field of evaluation of image generative models. I am not very familiar with the existing benchmarks and how superior the MMGen-Bench is compared to existing ones. However, I think the paper is well-written and the proposed pipeline makes a lot of sense to me. More specifically, it has the following advantages:
1. The benchmark is designed to evaluate image generation models conditioned on both text and reference images. Such unified benchmarks are lacking in the field.
2. The proposed evaluation metric AMS considers multiple aspects of the generated images including objects, relations, attributes, and counting. It is an automatic metric and aligns well with human preferences.
3. The evaluation of 17 image generative models is comprehensive.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. The benchmark does not have a metric measuring the diversity of the generated images.
2. A deeper analysis of the leaderboard would be expected. Such as the common practice of the winning models, regarding the training data, architecture, training protocols etc.
3. The calculation of AMS entails inference with Qwen-VL2.5-72B multiple times. This is super computationally expensive.  Can we get a similar result using a smaller model?
4. It would make the paper more self-contained if the authors could provide a brief introduction of the metrics such as CUTE, PAL4VST, Aesthetic, etc in the appendix.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

dataset_code_comments.value: The authors have uploaded the data and code to kaggle.

final_justification.value: During the rebuttal phase, the authors have addressed most of my concerns. I think the paper propose a comprehensive and intuitive evaluation framework for image generation, which is valuable. I would keep the positive score.

title.value: MMIG-Bench: Towards Comprehensive and Explainable Evaluation of Multi-Modal Image Generation Models

abstract.value: Recent multimodal image generators such as GPT-4o, Gemini 2.0 Flash, and Gemini 2.5 Pro excel at following complex instructions, editing images and maintaining concept consistency. However, they are still evaluated by disjoint toolkits: text-to-image (T2I) benchmarks that lacks multi-modal conditioning, and customized image generation benchmarks that overlook compositional semantics and common knowledge. We propose **MMIG-Bench**, a comprehensive **M**ulti-**M**odal **I**mage **G**eneration **Bench**mark that unifies these tasks by pairing 4,850 richly annotated text prompts with 1,750 multi-view reference images across 380 subjects, spanning humans, animals, objects, and artistic styles. **MMIG-Bench** is equipped with a three-level evaluation framework: (1) low-level metrics for visual artifacts and identity preservation of objects; (2) novel Aspect Matching Score (AMS): a VQA-based mid-level metric that delivers fine-grained prompt-image alignment and shows strong correlation with human judgments; and (3) high-level metrics for aesthetics and human preference. Using **MMIG-Bench**, we benchmark 17 state-of-the-art models, including Gemini 2.5 Pro, FLUX, DreamBooth, and IP-Adapter, and validate our metrics with 32k human ratings, yielding in-depth insights into architecture and data design.
